paras: The shooting of Willie Page took place on the Mobile, Alabama, river front, probably on 1 July 1903, when Special Policeman Jerry Lynch of the Louisville & Nashville Railroad fired into a crowd of Black boys and wounded 13-year-old Willie Page in the hip. The boy was treated and sent home, and the only report, in the Montgomery Advertiser, gave the officer's reason as an attempt to frighten two boys who were fighting.

Shortly before noon, Lynch, a special policeman employed by the railroad on the river front, shot into a group the paper called "a crowd of negro boys." The bullet struck Willie Page, aged 13, in the hip. According to the report, two of the boys had been fighting, and the officer was "said to have fired with intent to frighten them."
Page was attended by the city physician and sent to his home. No report of an arrest, hearing or discipline of Lynch appears in the coverage.

The shooting appeared as a brief item headed "Policeman Shoots Boy" in the Montgomery Advertiser of 2 July 1903, part of a letter from the paper's Mobile bureau. That letter led with the removal of four post-office employees, and its headline deck closed with "Policeman Shoots a Negro Boy." The item named the boys' race but not the officer's, and it passed on the officer's explanation as hearsay ("it is learned," "is said") without comment.
No other white paper and no Black newspaper was found to have carried the story.
